title: Other
text:
President, Duke Quantum Information Society · duquantum.org



The DuQuantum organizing team and sponsor representatives


DuQuantum 2026 was the first quantum computing hackathon ever held at Duke University. For 24 hours, more than 130 students in over 40 teams worked on quantum computing challenges, from complete beginners writing their first quantum circuits to advanced students tackling problems at the frontier of the field. I led the organizing team that put it together.

Two tracks. Participants chose an Intro Track or a Standard Track depending on their background, so newcomers and experienced students could both find the right challenge.
Six industry and academic challenges from IQM, Alice & Bob, BlueQubit, Google, the Duke Quantum Center (DQC), and Pasqal. DuQuantum was the first quantum hackathon Pasqal has sponsored.
Over $30,000 in sponsorships, with more than $4,000 in prizes awarded.
The first quantum computing hackathon to be a Major League Hacking (MLH) member event. We were also supported by IBM Quantum through Qiskit Fall Fest.







Opening ceremony







Keynote by Prof. Kenneth Brown: “How to Build a Quantum Computer”







Teams at work during the 24-hour hack





DuQuantum was made possible by our sponsors (Alice & Bob, Pasqal, BlueQubit, Google, IQM Quantum Computers, Classiq, Quandela, neQxt, the Duke Physics Department, and the Duke Rhodes Information Initiative), by faculty and staff of the Duke Quantum Center, and by an organizing team that worked on it for months. Most of all, it was made by the participants. We hope to see you all, and more, next year!

I’m an undergraduate at Duke University studying Physics and Mathematics, graduating in 2027. My interests sit where the two meet: quantum information science, where questions about what physical systems can compute turn out to be questions about structure, representation, and information.


I’m aiming toward graduate study in quantum information science, and I’m drawn to the theory side: quantum algorithms, error correction, and the representation-theoretic and information-theoretic tools that make them tractable. I’m equally interested in the near-term question of what today’s noisy hardware can genuinely be used for.

title: Can quantum-mechanical description of physical reality be considered complete?
text:
Abstract
In a complete theory there is an element corresponding to each element of reality. A sufficient condition for the reality of a physical quantity is the possibility of predicting it with certainty, without disturbing the system. In quantum mechanics in the case of two physical quantities described by non-commuting operators, the knowledge of one precludes the knowledge of the other. Then either (1) the description of reality given by the wave function in quantum mechanics is not complete or (2) these two quantities cannot have simultaneous reality. Consideration of the problem of making predictions concerning a system on the basis of measurements made on another system that had previously interacted with it leads to the result that if (1) is false then (2) is also false. One is thus led to conclude that the description of reality as given by a wave function is not complete.

I’m now starting a project on quantum information processing with indium atoms.

title: Research
Research
section: Detecting entanglement in scalar fields with majorization
text:
Detecting entanglement in scalar fields with majorization
Duke University · Advisor: Prof. Natalie Klco · August 2025 – Present
Background. How much entanglement exists between two separate, non-overlapping regions of a quantum scalar field, and how can we detect it? I’m studying whether majorization (a mathematical way of ordering probability distributions by how “spread out” they are) gives useful criteria for detecting that entanglement, and how the entanglement behaves in the continuum limit.

References

B. Gao and N. Klco, Detecting spacelike vacuum entanglement at all distances and promoting negativity to a necessary and sufficient entanglement measure in many-body regimes, Phys. Rev. A 112, 012430 (2025). doi:10.1103/m9w1-ppqz · arXiv:2410.04162

title: Research
section: Quantum error detection with Pauli checks
text:
Quantum error detection with Pauli checks
Argonne National Laboratory (DOE SULI) · Advisors: Dr. Zain Saleem and Dr. Ji Liu · May – December 2025
Background. Errors on today’s quantum computers can be caught by “sandwiching” part of a circuit between Pauli checks: extra operations that flag runs where an error occurred, so those runs can be thrown out. Real hardware noise is often biased, with some kinds of errors far more likely than others. How well do these checks hold up under biased noise, and how should a compiler use them?
My contributions. I implemented and benchmarked a Pauli-check error-detection protocol under biased noise models, to inform how QuantEM, a quantum error management compiler, applies error detection. The work is part of the QuantEM paper (arXiv:2509.15505), and I presented it as Automatic Quantum Error Detection with Pauli Checks at Argonne (August 2025). It also motivated an investigation into using deep learning models to characterize hardware noise.

References

A. Gonzales, R. Shaydulin, Z. H. Saleem, and M. Suchara, “Quantum error mitigation by Pauli check sandwiching,” Sci. Rep. 13, 2122 (2023).
D. M. Debroy and K. R. Brown, “Extended flag gadgets for low-overhead circuit verification,” Phys. Rev. A 102, 052409 (2020). doi:10.1103/PhysRevA.102.052409
E. van den Berg, S. Bravyi, J. M. Gambetta, P. Jurcevic, D. Maslov, and K. Temme, “Single-shot error mitigation by coherent Pauli checks,” Phys. Rev. Research 5, 033193 (2023).

title: Research
section: Faster quantum gates through pulse-level control
text:
Faster quantum gates through pulse-level control
North Carolina State University · Advisor: Prof. Lex Kemper · July – August 2023
Background. On superconducting quantum computers, each gate is ultimately a microwave pulse, and qubits decohere over time, so longer circuits accumulate more error. Can we shorten circuits by working directly at the pulse level instead of assembling every operation from a fixed set of native gates?
My contributions. Using Qiskit Pulse on IBM backends, I built parametrized gates by scaling the calibrated microwave pulses (single-qubit drives and the cross-resonance pulses inside the two-qubit ECR gate) instead of decomposing rotations into standard gate sequences. I checked that the pulse-scaled rotations matched the conventional gates’ accuracy, then used them to simulate the time evolution of a 3-qubit spin system.
Results. Operations ran about 60% faster. Shorter execution let us simulate the system to longer times: the pulse-level circuits tracked the ideal magnetization dynamics noticeably longer than the conventionally compiled ones.






Calibrated X(π) pulse on a single qubit







ECR gate: cross-resonance pulses with an echo

References

P. Gokhale, A. Javadi-Abhari, N. Earnest, Y. Shi, and F. T. Chong, “Optimized quantum compilation for near-term algorithms with OpenPulse,” arXiv:2004.11205v2 [quant-ph] (2020). arXiv:2004.11205
J. P. T. Stenger, N. T. Bronn, D. J. Egger, and D. Pekker, “Simulating the dynamics of braiding of Majorana zero modes using an IBM quantum computer,” Phys. Rev. Research 3, 033171 (2021).

title: Research
section: Interfacial free energy of soft matter with molecular dynamics
text:
Interfacial free energy of soft matter with molecular dynamics
Duke University · Advisor: Prof. Gaurav Arya · June 2026 – Present


Background. When a particle sits at an interface, its free energy depends on how it is oriented. Mapping that orientational free energy landscape tells us which orientations a soft matter system prefers, and how strongly.
My contributions. I implemented a data-driven model to map the orientational interfacial free energy landscape. To build it, I run molecular dynamics simulations in LAMMPS across many physical configurations, parallelized on an HPC Slurm cluster, and compute potentials of mean force with umbrella sampling to characterize the system’s thermodynamics.



Molecular dynamics simulation with the particle’s orientation constrained.



References

U. Gupta, T. Hanrath, and F. A. Escobedo, “Modeling the orientational and positional behavior of polyhedral nanoparticles at fluid-fluid interfaces,” Phys. Rev. Materials 1, 055602 (2017). doi:10.1103/PhysRevMaterials.1.055602
Y. Zhou, T.-Y. Tang, B. H.-J. Lee, and G. Arya, “Tunable orientation and assembly of polymer-grafted nanocubes at fluid–fluid interfaces,” ACS Nano 16, 7457–7470 (2022). doi:10.1021/acsnano.1c10416
Y. Zhou, Ş. Çallıoğlu, and G. Arya, “From frustration to order: Role of fluid–fluid interfaces in precision assembly of nanoparticles,” Langmuir 40, 26800–26810 (2024). doi:10.1021/acs.langmuir.4c03321
